newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran presidential candidate backs renewed U.S. ties.
newsitem.headline: Iran presidential candidate backs renewed U.S. ties.

text.p: A liberal Iranian opposition figure who plans to run in presidential elections next month has said he will establish ties with the United States if he is elected, Iran's official news agency IRNA said on Friday.

It quoted Ezzatollah Sahabi, a liberal Islamist critic of government policies, as telling reporters in Tehran he would resume relations with Washington "if that is not going to make Iran in any way dependent on the United States".
Sahabi said his pre-conditions were that "the United States must pull out of the Persian Gulf and agree to talks in a peaceful atmosphere", the agency said.
Iran on Thursday began registering candidates for the May 23 elections to replace President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.
Candidates will be screened by the Guardian Council, a body of lawyers and Shi'ite Moslem clerics which in past elections disqualified all but a handful of those who signed up.

Sahabi, a former head of the state Plan and Budget Organisation, has said he will run on a platform advocating easing tensions in Iran's foreign relations and guaranteeing freedom and security for Iranians at home.
Conservative Parliament Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri and Mohammad Khatami, a former minister of culture, appear to be the front-runners among a dozen hopefuls who have said they would sign up.
Khatami is backed by pro-Rafsanjani centrists and radical Islamist intellectuals who have moderated many of their views in recent years.
Iran's laws say only Shi'ite men can become candidates, but a female former member of parliament has said she will sign up to bring about a legal interpretation allowing women to run.
Rafsanjani is barred by the constitution from running for a third consecutive four-year term.

The United States broke diplomatic ties with Iran in April 1980, five months after militant Islamist students stormed the U.S. embassy in Tehran, taking 52 Americans hostage. The hostage crisis lasted 444 days.
